claims.text: The starting alloy is equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
As-cast equimolar CoCrFeNiTi is a highly or fully disordered simple solid solution with minimal short-range order.
The starting alloy has relatively large grains.
As-cast equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has relatively low hardness and yield strength.
As-cast equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has favorable plasticity and machinability.
A random atomic distribution permits easy dislocation glide in the as-cast alloy.
The scarcity of local obstacles to dislocation motion causes the relatively low hardness and strength of the as-cast alloy.
Aging at 500–600 °C for 1–10 hours will promote short-range atomic ordering in CoCrFeNiTi.
The proposed aging window can produce short-range order without significant precipitation or phase separation.
Short-range-ordered regions create localized lattice distortions.
The localized lattice distortions associated with short-range order pin or obstruct dislocations.
Increased atomic ordering raises yield strength by impeding dislocation motion.
Short-range ordering produced by aging will increase hardness relative to the as-cast alloy.
Short-range ordering produced by aging will increase compressive yield strength relative to the as-cast alloy.
Increasing atomic order will moderately reduce ductility.
The magnitude of strengthening will correlate with the measured extent of short-range order.
The hypothesis is limited to equimolar or near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a simple solid-solution state, aged at 500–600 °C and tested in quasi-static compression from 25 °C to 600 °C.
At substantially higher aging temperatures or sufficiently long durations, precipitation hardening may replace short-range-order strengthening as the dominant mechanism.

Comparing as-cast and aged samples while measuring short-range order, secondary phases, hardness, compressive yield strength, and plastic strain can distinguish short-range-order strengthening from precipitation strengthening.
Confirmed short-range order without a significant mechanical-property change, or strengthening clearly attributable to precipitation, would falsify the proposed mechanism.
